You’ve probably lied to someone today. You also probably think you lie less than everyone else. Welp, I have some bad news. We all manipulate, we all get played, and sometimes, the smarter you are, the easier you are to con.

In this episode, Drew and I get into what manipulation is, why everyone does it, and how to keep from getting fooled. You can’t fully escape influence, and you might not want to. But once you know the playbook, you’ll spot it, even when it’s coming from inside the house.

Forgetting to hit send and launching a business that flops both count as failure, but they shouldn't get the same reaction. Drew and I wrap up this episode through a story of a young Harvard researcher who found that the best hospital teams reported the most mistakes. She thought she'd botched her research, until she realized what was really going on. Her work gives us three types of failure: the kind to fix and forget, the kind to catch early, and the kind worth chasing for the lesson. We also share why a failed startup barely improves your odds the second time, five questions that tell you whether it's time to quit, and why the right moment to quit almost always feels too early.

Casanova had more adventures than anyone in recorded history. He escaped an inescapable prison, ran France's first lottery, slept with over 120 women, and met Voltaire, the Pope, and Benjamin Franklin. He also died broke, alone, and forgotten in a small castle in present-day Slovakia. We use his life as the cautionary tale of what Kierkegaard called the aesthetic stage, where novelty becomes an addiction and every open door is another reason to never walk through one. Confidence isn't something you build. It's what's left over. You've done the pose. Hands on hips, chest out, an affirmation on a sticky note stuck to the mirror. And then you walked into the room feeling exactly the same, or worse. Here's what nobody tells you: the entire concept of confidence you've been sold was invented by an anxious preacher in the 1940s who mistook his own coping mechanism for a universal law. In this episode we trace where it all went wrong, from Norman Vincent Peale to power poses to the self-esteem movement that quietly failed a whole generation. Confidence only helps you when it matches your actual ability, and Florence Foster Jenkins is the proof. In 1944 she sold out Carnegie Hall, with a two-month waiting list for tickets. She also could not sing a single note in tune, and she had no idea. In chapter three, Drew and I use her story to get at the real problem with confidence: calibration. Tip too far one way and you get the Dunning-Kruger effect, where the people who know the least are the surest of themselves, including a bank robber who covered his face in lemon juice because he thought it would make him invisible to cameras. Tip the other way and you get imposter syndrome, which turns out to show up most in high performers. We get into the McKinsey study that found future superstars are basically overachievers with crippling insecurities, the spotlight effect and the time I walked the Venice boardwalk in a chicken suit to prove nobody's watching, and why narcissism has almost nothing to do with confidence and everything to do with an inability to take feedback. The goal was never to feel as confident as possible. It's to see yourself clearly.

Where does confidence actually come from? Not from thinking your way into it. Bandura took people with life-crippling phobias and, in a single afternoon, walked them from terror to holding snakes in their laps. The twist: those people didn't only lose the fear.
